rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: OpenAI just gave healthcare AI the ability to actually *do* things — not answer questions, but click through software, fill out forms, move across systems. That's a different animal entirely.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And they dropped more than twenty new plugins on the same day. That's not an update, that's a statement.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The statement being: we would like to be inside your hospital's software stack before anyone asks permission.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We'll get into what that means. November 17th, 2026.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. Three stories today, starting with the one in the title: OpenAI's clinical agents and what they can actually do now.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the headline. November 16th, OpenAI announces computer-use agents, improved clinical search, and more than twenty healthcare plugins in ChatGPT for Healthcare. What actually changed here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The key phrase is "computer-use agent." That's not a chatbot. That's software that can operate other software — navigate a screen, click through menus, fill in fields.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Like a person doing data entry, but it's the AI doing it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. Previously, ChatGPT for Healthcare would *answer* a clinical question. Now it can theoretically go into an existing system and *execute* something inside it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: OpenAI framed this specifically around reducing manual workflow burden. Prior authorization forms, moving patient records between systems — the administrative layer that burns out half the people in healthcare.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Prior authorization. Explain that for people who haven't had the joy.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So before a patient can get a procedure or a medication covered, a clinician has to submit paperwork to the insurer proving it's medically necessary. It's often a stack of forms, dozens of fields, done manually, every single time.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And that's what the agent might handle.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: In theory. This is a product announcement, not a clinical trial result. OpenAI says it's designed for that — they haven't published error rates on legacy medical record systems.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the part that matters to me. Healthcare software is notoriously fragmented. Some hospitals are still running systems from fifteen years ago. Can an AI agent actually navigate that?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: OpenAI says it works with existing healthcare software. Which is a careful phrase.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: "Works with" is doing a lot of load in that sentence.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. It doesn't say it integrates seamlessly. It says it's designed to operate across those environments. Whether your specific EHR — your electronic health record system — is on that list, that's the question for your IT team.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I keep thinking about what happens when the agent makes a wrong move. In a form for, I don't know, a marketing campaign, a mistake is fixable. In a clinical record —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the safety question that this announcement doesn't fully answer. This is not a regulatory approval for medical decision-making. OpenAI is explicit about that.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And it shouldn't be confused with one. What it is, is a workflow tool. It's meant to handle the administrative scaffolding, not diagnose.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does that distinction hold in practice, though? Because if an agent is pulling information from a clinical record to populate a form, it's reading clinical data. The line blurs.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It does blur. And that's where the safety and results reporting OpenAI paired with this announcement matters — they flagged it, which at least means they're not pretending it's a simple tool.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll tell you what I find actually interesting from a healthcare system perspective. The plugin count. More than twenty new integrations. That means OpenAI is building connective tissue between itself and the existing software ecosystem that hospitals already use.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Instead of asking hospitals to replace what they have.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which nobody is going to do. Healthcare procurement cycles are measured in years. So if you want to be inside a hospital workflow in 2026, you don't sell them a new system — you become a layer on top of the systems they already can't get rid of.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's genuinely smart. Annoying, but smart.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Annoying how?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Because it makes the dependency invisible. The hospital thinks it's still running its own system. OpenAI is now part of how that system functions.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Though to be fair, that's how every successful enterprise software integration works. Salesforce didn't replace email, it connected to it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I keep circling back to — the clinical search improvement. That's the quieter part of this announcement. It's not just the agents doing things; it's how the system finds information before it acts on it. If the search is wrong, everything downstream is wrong.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And "trusted clinical search" is OpenAI's phrase, not an independent certification. We don't know what sources it's pulling from or how conflicts between sources get resolved.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's actually the more immediate risk than the agent behavior. A prior auth form filled out confidently on a flawed literature pull is worse than a form left blank.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the agent being capable isn't the whole question. It's capable *based on what*.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. The search quality and the execution quality are two separate things that have to both work, in sequence, for this to be safe in practice.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which nobody in the announcement separated out clearly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Should they have?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I think they should have, yes. Those are different failure modes with different consequences.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: One is an information problem. One is an action problem. Collapsing them into "workflow tool" obscures where the actual risk sits.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So for anyone evaluating this — that's your first question. Not just can it use our software, but what is it reading before it does.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the one I'd want answered before anything else.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fair point. What should a clinician or an IT lead actually do with this announcement today?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'd say the first question is: does this work with *your* specific software stack? The claim is broad. The practical answer depends on your environment. Test it in a low-stakes workflow before you put it anywhere near patient-facing records.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And whoever owns procurement should probably be asking about liability. If the agent mis-populates a form, who carries that? OpenAI hasn't published anything about indemnification in healthcare settings that I've seen from this announcement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the question that'll be answered in the first legal filing, unfortunately.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why you don't wait for the first legal filing to ask it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Exactly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So for anyone evaluating this today — the administrative capability is real and moving. The clinical liability framework is not yet in place. Those two things need to close before anyone should trust it near patient-facing records.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. Google added Gemini-powered agents directly into AdMob on November 16th. AdMob is Google's ad platform for mobile app developers — it's how they make money from advertising. Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture the trading floor at a large asset manager in New York — mid-morning, someone has the Alphabet earnings model open and they're watching one line in the revenue bridge that just keeps growing: mobile advertising. AdMob isn't glamorous, but it's the quiet engine under a significant portion of the mobile economy. What Google announced is called Ask AdMob — a conversational agent built with Gemini that lives directly inside a developer's AdMob account. And the tools alongside it, the agent skills and an MCP server, those are the parts that let it actually *act* inside a developer's setup rather than just answer questions about it. The institutional read is straightforward: Google is making it substantially harder to leave the ecosystem. Not by locking the door. By making the door more useful than any alternative.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus, you're describing it like it's a chess match. For a developer with one small app, isn't this just — a thing that might fix their error faster at eleven at night?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Yes. And both things can be true simultaneously. That developer genuinely benefits. Google also benefits from that developer never seriously evaluating a competitor.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story. What is an MCP server and why does it show up here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: MCP — Model Context Protocol — is basically a standard for connecting an AI to live tools and data. So instead of the agent only knowing what's in its training, the MCP server lets it reach into your actual account, your analytics, your settings, and act on them.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So it's not just reading your AdMob account. It's doing things inside it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the design. Fixing integration errors, auditing brand safety settings, adjusting your setup. Things you'd otherwise click through manually or wait on a support ticket for.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Brand safety — say what that means quickly.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Whether your ads appear next to content that would embarrass whoever paid for them. A car company doesn't want their ad next to footage of a crash. It's a real, expensive problem in mobile advertising. Google says the agent can audit those settings.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is genuinely useful if it works. Brand safety audits can take a team days.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: You'd use it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Anyone would.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, but I want to push on how much the agent is actually *deciding* versus flagging for a human.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Google hasn't published specifics about where human approval is required. The framing — helping developers build, fix, and grow — implies it's taking real actions, not just making recommendations. But the exact decision boundary isn't in what they announced.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that's the question developers should be asking before they hand it their monetization settings. Not because Google is acting in bad faith. Because knowing what an agent can do on its own is basic operational hygiene.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does any of this matter to a developer who's not already in the Google ad ecosystem?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Probably not immediately. The tools work inside AdMob. Different network, different story. But if the friction reduction is real, it makes AdMob a more compelling place to be going forward.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I'm still sitting with — the agent skills. That's listed separately from Ask AdMob. What's the actual difference?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So Ask AdMob is the conversational layer — you type a question, it responds. Agent skills are discrete actions it can run. Think of it like the difference between asking a colleague what's wrong with your setup versus handing them the keyboard.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the MCP server is what connects those skills to your live data.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. Without that connection, the agent is guessing based on general knowledge. With it, it's looking at your actual numbers and acting on them.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a meaningful distinction for a developer trying to diagnose why their fill rate dropped at two in the morning.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fill rate — that's how often an ad slot actually gets an ad in it?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Yes. Empty slot, no revenue. Developers watch it obsessively.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that's genuinely the pain point Google is targeting. Not the glamorous part of monetization — the part where something silently breaks and you don't find out until you check your dashboard.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the question I haven't heard answered is — does the agent tell you it changed something, or do you find out from the dashboard?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Google hasn't specified that. The announcement describes it acting on your setup. The notification behavior isn't detailed.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's not a small thing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: No. That's the difference between a helpful colleague and one who rearranges your desk while you sleep.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Quietly. With good intentions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And technically better cable management.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Heh. Still, I'd want the email. Which is precisely the point. Google doesn't need to be aggressive about lock-in when usefulness does the same job more quietly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That might be the most diplomatic thing you've said about a large tech company.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm choosing my moments.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Jamie, collecting AI headlines is becoming a full-time occupation. I rather suspect nobody budgeted for that department.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is where The Ledger comes in. Five focused briefings help you sort the news and consider what it means for your next decision.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger, then. Less collecting headlines, more asking what actually matters before the next meeting?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly the idea. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Let's get back to the discussion.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story, and I'll say it plainly — this one feels different in kind from the other two. November 16th, OpenAI announced it's expanding free access to its frontier models for two hundred thousand academic researchers worldwide.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Two hundred thousand. That's not a pilot program.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It's not. And they paired it with a separate report on how more than eighteen hundred scientists are already using ChatGPT in research. So there's existing evidence of adoption, and now they're scaling it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: What does "frontier model" mean for someone who isn't inside this world?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The most capable models OpenAI has. Not the lite versions or the free tier — the ones researchers and enterprises typically pay for. That's what they're giving academic researchers at no cost.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which matters because a lot of research institutions, especially outside wealthy universities in the US or Europe, have been effectively priced out.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's the part I keep coming back to. A lab in Nairobi or Chennai with a small budget but serious researchers — this potentially changes what they can do with their work.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: OpenAI's framing is scientific productivity. AI as a tool for the actual research process, not just writing assistance.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that distinction matters. When people hear "AI in research" they often think — someone using it to write an abstract.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which, to be clear, people are absolutely doing.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Yes, fine, but the ambition here is bigger. Using frontier models to analyze data, design experiments, synthesize literature across fields you don't have time to fully read.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a genuinely different category of usefulness.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does access alone change what research can do, though? If the model is good but a researcher doesn't know how to use it well —

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's real. There's a capability gap between having access and knowing how to get useful results. But I'd rather that gap exist than have people without access *and* without skills.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Agreed. The floor matters. Though I'd be less than honest if I didn't note that two hundred thousand researchers building their workflows around OpenAI's models is not *only* a charitable act.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: There it is.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm not saying it's cynical. I'm saying it's strategic *and* beneficial. Those aren't mutually exclusive.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: They're really not. And I think — actually, the question I find more interesting than the strategy is the downstream effect on peer review. If thousands of papers are suddenly being partially produced or analyzed with AI assistance, what does that do to reproducibility?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Meaning — can another researcher reproduce your results if one of your steps was an AI call that might give a different answer next time?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly. If the model updates, if its behavior changes —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's already a live problem in the field. Researchers have been writing about how to cite model versions, how to log the exact prompts used, so that another scientist can actually recreate the step.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And this expansion might accelerate that problem before the norms are in place to handle it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Maybe. Or it might force the norms into place faster because now there are two hundred thousand people who need them.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Scaled-up problems do tend to generate scaled-up solutions, eventually.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: OpenAI's report on the eighteen hundred scientists who are already using this — did they publish specifics on what kinds of research?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The announcement linked to a broader science and research report but didn't break it down by field in the summary we have. So we know scientists are using it; we don't know if it's distributed across biology, materials science, social science, or concentrated somewhere specific.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which would change how to interpret it. A hundred climate researchers using it is different news than a hundred economists.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Fair. What's the practical thing for a researcher listening right now?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Check whether you're eligible for the program. The access is for academic researchers — there are eligibility criteria, it's not open to everyone. If you qualify and you're not using frontier models because of cost, the barrier just moved.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the methodological question is real — start thinking now about how you document AI-assisted steps. Not because the work is less valid, but because reproducibility is what makes it science rather than just interesting output.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's actually a useful frame. The tool is only as good as your documentation of how you used it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is true of every tool, honestly. It's just easier to forget with AI because it feels like thinking.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Hm. That's the most unsettling thing you've said all episode.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You're welcome.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The question today is not whether the tool saves the word. It is whether you can design a fair test of that before you need the answer at eleven PM the night before the show.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Okay, that is a different question.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Thank you, Rufus.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: He folds fast when there is a deadline involved.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I contain multitudes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The proposed workflow is hypothetical. This is a scenario, not a result anyone has measured. Adobe documents Enhance Speech as a web-based tool that takes, in Adobe's language, just minutes to clean up audio files. What the documentation does not cover is comic timing. That part is on you.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So what does a fair test actually look like?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You record one fifteen-second line. Your own voice, something with a deliberate pause before the final word. Fan running in the room. Keep the original file. Process a copy through Enhance Speech. Level-match the playback before you let anyone hear them, because louder sounds better and better is not the same as clearer.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Level-matching feels like the step people skip.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is absolutely the step people skip. And then they conclude the processed version won, when really it was just turned up slightly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Who listens to the comparison?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Someone who has not seen the script. You play both versions unlabeled and ask two questions separately. First: what was the last word? Second: did the pause feel like a pause or just a gap?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Those are not the same question.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: They are genuinely not. A listener who gets the word right but says the timing felt soft has told you something the intelligibility score cannot.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And if both versions lose the word entirely?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Then neither file is the answer, and the answer is a different recording position. The fan does not always lose. That is a legitimate conclusion, not a defeat.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the AI makes a decision, and the human audits the joke.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly that. No guaranteed improvement. The fictional rehearsal scenario is untested. Adobe documents the enhancement; the comedy is empirical.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: First step for someone who wants to run this comparison?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: One line, your own voice, web upload at podcast.adobe.com. Check your file limits before you start. Enhancement strength is adjustable with a Premium account, but the basic comparison does not require it. Keep the original. That is non-negotiable.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Keep the original because the fan might have been right all along.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Keep the original because you need to know what the joke was supposed to sound like. The tool does not know. Only you do.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The after-the-story segment, now with homework.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I am genuinely going to run this test.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the most hopeful thing said here today.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing that sits across all three stories today — the word 'agentic.' It kept coming up. What does it actually mean when you're not in a lab?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It means the AI isn't waiting to be asked. It's taking a step inside another system on your behalf. That's genuinely different from a search result or a draft.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the accountability question that comes with it is different too. When something goes wrong in a workflow an agent ran, the trail is harder to follow than when a person clicked the button.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which is why the watch items are all variations of the same underlying question: not whether the AI can answer, but whether anyone has agreed on what happens when it acts and gets it wrong.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What to watch next — for healthcare, the liability framework. That's the gap between the product announcement and actual clinical deployment. For AdMob, watch how much autonomy developers actually give the agent versus keeping a human in the loop for monetization decisions. For the researcher program — watch whether major journals publish updated reproducibility standards in the next six months.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Also — NVIDIA earnings tomorrow. November 17th. We flagged this two weeks ago. First real signal on whether the infrastructure thesis that's been funding all of this holds.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That one will tell us a lot.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'll be here tomorrow, probably not on a trading floor, definitely with opinions.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: If your doctor used an AI agent to handle your medical paperwork, would you be more concerned about privacy or more relieved by the efficiency?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us next episode for what changes next.
